notes_list.title: Economics
notes_list.basic_overview: Economics studies how individuals, firms and governments make choices about the use of scarce resources to satisfy human wants.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Economics broadly deals with production, consumption, distribution, exchange, resource allocation and the choices created by scarcity.

notes_list.title: Scarcity and Choice
notes_list.basic_overview: Human wants are numerous while resources are limited. Scarcity therefore requires individuals and societies to make choices.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Every choice involves an opportunity cost because selecting one alternative generally means giving up another alternative.

notes_list.title: Opportunity Cost
notes_list.basic_overview: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made.
notes_list.extra_info_content: For example, choosing to study for an examination instead of working may involve the income that could have been earned as the opportunity cost.

notes_list.title: Land
notes_list.basic_overview: Land represents natural resources used in production, including soil, forests, minerals, water and other natural resources.
notes_list.extra_info_content: In economics, land is treated as a factor of production whose supply is generally considered fixed in physical terms.

notes_list.title: Labour
notes_list.basic_overview: Labour refers to the physical and mental effort contributed by people in the production of goods and services.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The quality of labour is influenced by education, training, health, skills and experience.

notes_list.title: Capital
notes_list.basic_overview: Capital consists of produced resources such as machinery, tools, buildings and equipment that are used to produce other goods and services.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Capital is different from money itself. In production theory, physical capital refers to productive assets.

notes_list.title: Entrepreneurship
notes_list.basic_overview: Entrepreneurship involves organizing factors of production, making business decisions and bearing risks associated with production.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Entrepreneurs coordinate resources, introduce innovations and make decisions about production and investment.

notes_list.title: Law of Demand
notes_list.basic_overview: Other things remaining constant, quantity demanded generally decreases when price rises and increases when price falls.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded is represented by a downward-sloping demand curve under standard assumptions.

notes_list.title: Determinants of Demand
notes_list.basic_overview: Demand is influenced by factors such as income, prices of related goods, tastes and preferences, population and expectations.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A change in the good's own price generally causes movement along the demand curve, while changes in other determinants can shift the demand curve.

notes_list.title: Price Elasticity of Demand
notes_list.basic_overview: Price elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the price of a good.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Elasticity can be expressed as percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price.

notes_list.title: Law of Supply
notes_list.basic_overview: Other things remaining constant, quantity supplied generally increases when price rises and decreases when price falls.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The relationship between price and quantity supplied is generally represented by an upward-sloping supply curve.

notes_list.title: Determinants of Supply
notes_list.basic_overview: Supply is influenced by input prices, technology, taxes, subsidies, number of sellers, expectations and natural conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A change in the good's own price generally causes movement along the supply curve, whereas other determinants can shift the supply curve.

notes_list.title: Market
notes_list.basic_overview: A market is a system or arrangement through which buyers and sellers interact to exchange goods and services.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Markets may be physical or digital and can differ according to competition, number of sellers, product differentiation and barriers to entry.

notes_list.title: Equilibrium Price
notes_list.basic_overview: Market equilibrium occurs when quantity demanded equals quantity supplied at a particular price.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A shortage tends to create upward pressure on price, while a surplus tends to create downward pressure, assuming other conditions remain unchanged.

notes_list.title: Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
notes_list.basic_overview: GDP measures the monetary value of final goods and services produced within the economic territory of a country during a specified period.
notes_list.extra_info_content: GDP can be measured using production, income and expenditure approaches, subject to appropriate accounting identities and adjustments.

notes_list.title: Real and Nominal GDP
notes_list.basic_overview: Nominal GDP is measured at current prices, while real GDP adjusts output measures to remove the effect of price changes.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Real GDP is useful for comparing changes in the volume of production over time.

notes_list.title: Planning Commission
notes_list.basic_overview: The Planning Commission was established in 1950 to formulate plans for economic development and resource allocation.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015.

notes_list.title: Five Year Plans
notes_list.basic_overview: India adopted a system of Five Year Plans after independence to organize development priorities and investment.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The First Five Year Plan began in 1951 and placed considerable emphasis on agriculture, irrigation and related development.

notes_list.title: Agriculture in Indian Economy
notes_list.basic_overview: Agriculture remains an important part of India's economy through food production, employment, raw materials and rural livelihoods.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Agricultural performance is affected by monsoon conditions, irrigation, technology, input availability, market access and government policies.

notes_list.title: Green Revolution
notes_list.basic_overview: The Green Revolution involved the adoption of high-yielding varieties, irrigation, fertilizers, pesticides and improved agricultural practices.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The major early gains were concentrated in wheat and rice and were particularly significant in regions with suitable irrigation and infrastructure.

notes_list.title: Agricultural Marketing
notes_list.basic_overview: Agricultural marketing includes the processes involved in assembling, storing, transporting, processing and selling agricultural produce.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Market infrastructure, storage facilities, transportation, information and institutional arrangements influence farmers' access to markets.

notes_list.title: Industrialization
notes_list.basic_overview: Industrialization involves the expansion and diversification of manufacturing and other productive activities.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Industrial development can increase productivity, create employment, support exports and generate demand for infrastructure and services.

notes_list.title: Small Scale and MSME Sector
notes_list.basic_overview: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises form an important part of India's productive economy and contribute to employment, entrepreneurship and supply chains.
notes_list.extra_info_content: MSMEs operate across manufacturing and services and may face challenges involving finance, technology, market access and infrastructure.

notes_list.title: Growth of Service Sector
notes_list.basic_overview: The service sector includes activities such as trade, transport, communication, finance, education, healthcare, information technology and professional services.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Expansion of services has been an important component of India's structural transformation and economic growth.

notes_list.title: Information Technology and IT-enabled Services
notes_list.basic_overview: India's information technology and IT-enabled services sector has developed significantly through software services, business-process services and digital technologies.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The sector contributes to exports, employment, innovation and the development of digital infrastructure.

notes_list.title: Transport Infrastructure
notes_list.basic_overview: Transport infrastructure includes roads, railways, ports, airports and other systems that facilitate movement of people and goods.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Efficient transport infrastructure reduces transaction costs, improves market connectivity and supports regional economic integration.

notes_list.title: Energy Infrastructure
notes_list.basic_overview: Energy infrastructure includes systems for electricity generation, transmission, distribution and fuel supply.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Reliable and affordable energy is important for households, agriculture, industry and services.

notes_list.title: Economic Reforms of 1991
notes_list.basic_overview: India introduced major economic reforms in 1991 involving changes in industrial policy, trade policy, investment rules and financial-sector arrangements.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The reform process is commonly described through liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation, although reforms covered a wide range of policy areas.

notes_list.title: Liberalisation
notes_list.basic_overview: Liberalisation refers to reducing or simplifying certain government restrictions and controls over economic activities.
notes_list.extra_info_content: In India, reforms included changes to industrial licensing, trade restrictions, investment rules and financial-sector regulation.

notes_list.title: Globalisation
notes_list.basic_overview: Globalisation refers to increasing economic integration among countries through trade, investment, technology and movement of services and information.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Greater integration can expand access to international markets and technology while also increasing exposure to international competition.

notes_list.title: Inflation
notes_list.basic_overview: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services over time, which reduces the purchasing power of money.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Inflation can be measured using different price indices. Its causes may include demand pressures, supply shocks, changes in costs and monetary conditions.

notes_list.title: Consumer Price Index
notes_list.basic_overview: The Consumer Price Index measures changes over time in the prices paid for a representative basket of consumer goods and services.
notes_list.extra_info_content: CPI-based inflation is widely used for assessing changes in consumer prices and purchasing power.

notes_list.title: Unemployment
notes_list.basic_overview: Unemployment refers to a situation in which people who are available for and seeking work do not have employment.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Different forms include frictional, structural, cyclical and seasonal unemployment. Definitions and measurement methods can vary across statistical systems.

notes_list.title: Disguised Unemployment
notes_list.basic_overview: Disguised unemployment occurs when more workers are engaged in an activity than are actually required, so removing some workers may have little or no effect on total output.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The concept is often discussed in relation to labour-intensive agricultural activities and low-productivity employment.

notes_list.title: Functions of Money
notes_list.basic_overview: Money performs important functions including medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Money removes the need for a direct double coincidence of wants required in barter and facilitates transactions in an economy.

notes_list.title: Commercial Banks
notes_list.basic_overview: Commercial banks accept deposits, provide loans and offer various payment and financial services.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Bank lending contributes to the creation of deposits and supports economic activity, subject to regulatory and financial constraints.

notes_list.title: Reserve Bank of India
notes_list.basic_overview: The Reserve Bank of India is India's central bank and performs functions related to monetary policy, currency management, banking regulation and financial stability.
notes_list.extra_info_content: RBI also acts as banker to the government and banker to banks and manages foreign exchange reserves under the applicable legal framework.

notes_list.title: Monetary Policy
notes_list.basic_overview: Monetary policy refers to actions undertaken by a central bank to influence monetary and financial conditions in the economy.
notes_list.extra_info_content: In India, the RBI's monetary policy framework uses the policy repo rate and other instruments to pursue specified objectives, including maintaining price stability while keeping growth in mind.

notes_list.title: Repo Rate
notes_list.basic_overview: The repo rate is the rate at which the central bank provides short-term liquidity to eligible financial institutions against eligible securities under the relevant framework.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Changes in policy rates can influence borrowing costs, financial conditions, aggregate demand and inflation, although the transmission process takes time.

notes_list.title: Fiscal Policy
notes_list.basic_overview: Fiscal policy concerns government decisions relating to taxation, expenditure and borrowing.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Fiscal policy can influence aggregate demand, public investment, redistribution and the provision of public goods and services.

notes_list.title: Fiscal Deficit
notes_list.basic_overview: Fiscal deficit represents the excess of total government expenditure over total receipts excluding borrowings during a specified period.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Fiscal deficit indicates the borrowing requirement of the government for financing the gap between expenditure and non-borrowed receipts.

notes_list.title: Balance of Payments
notes_list.basic_overview: The balance of payments records economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world over a specified period.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Major components include the current account and financial account, along with relevant capital and reserve transactions according to the accounting framework.

notes_list.title: Foreign Exchange Rate
notes_list.basic_overview: The foreign exchange rate represents the price of one currency expressed in terms of another currency.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Exchange rates are influenced by demand and supply for currencies, interest rates, inflation expectations, trade flows, capital flows and policy conditions.

notes_list.title: Poverty
notes_list.basic_overview: Poverty refers to inadequate command over resources needed to achieve minimum acceptable standards of living.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Poverty can be studied through income or consumption measures as well as multidimensional indicators covering education, health, living conditions and other dimensions.

notes_list.title: Poverty Alleviation
notes_list.basic_overview: Poverty alleviation involves policies and programmes aimed at improving incomes, employment, access to basic services and living conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Approaches include employment generation, social protection, access to education and healthcare, financial inclusion and infrastructure development.

notes_list.title: Human Development
notes_list.basic_overview: Human development focuses on expanding people's capabilities and opportunities to lead lives they value.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Important dimensions include health, education, income and broader capabilities. Economic growth and human development are related but are not identical concepts.

notes_list.title: Human Development Index
notes_list.basic_overview: The Human Development Index combines indicators related to health, education and standard of living to provide a broad measure of human development.
notes_list.extra_info_content: HDI uses life expectancy, education indicators and gross national income per capita as its three broad dimensions.

notes_list.title: Income Inequality
notes_list.basic_overview: Income inequality refers to differences in income received by individuals or households within an economy.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Inequality can be measured using tools such as the Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient, depending on the available data and methodology.

notes_list.title: Wealth Inequality
notes_list.basic_overview: Wealth inequality refers to differences in ownership of assets and net wealth across individuals or households.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Wealth includes accumulated assets such as property and financial assets after accounting for liabilities.

notes_list.title: Employment
notes_list.basic_overview: Employment refers to engagement in productive economic activity in return for wages, salaries, profits or other forms of remuneration.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Employment may be classified by sector, occupation, formal or informal status, and nature of work.

notes_list.title: Formal and Informal Employment
notes_list.basic_overview: Formal employment is generally associated with recognized employment arrangements and applicable legal and social protection systems, while informal employment may lack some of these protections.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The distinction depends on the statistical and institutional definition being used. Informal work represents a substantial part of employment in many developing economies.

notes_list.title: Sustainable Development
notes_list.basic_overview: Sustainable development seeks to meet present needs while maintaining the environmental, economic and social conditions required by future generations.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Sustainable development involves balancing economic development, social inclusion and environmental protection.

notes_list.title: Sustainable Development Goals
notes_list.basic_overview: The Sustainable Development Goals are a set of 17 global goals adopted by UN member states as part of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The goals cover areas including poverty, hunger, health, education, gender equality, clean energy, decent work, climate action and institutions.

notes_list.title: Direct Taxes
notes_list.basic_overview: Direct taxes are taxes whose burden is generally intended to fall directly on the person or entity legally liable to pay them.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Income tax and corporate income tax are examples of direct taxes in the Indian tax system.

notes_list.title: Indirect Taxes
notes_list.basic_overview: Indirect taxes are generally collected from one party but may be passed on through prices to other participants in the economy.
notes_list.extra_info_content: GST is an important example of an indirect tax in India.

notes_list.title: GST
notes_list.basic_overview: Goods and Services Tax is a destination-based indirect tax on the supply of goods and services in India, subject to the applicable rules and exemptions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: GST was introduced in India on 1 July 2017. The system includes Central GST, State GST and Integrated GST for different categories of transactions.

notes_list.title: Union Budget
notes_list.basic_overview: The Union Budget presents the government's estimated receipts and expenditure for a financial year along with taxation and policy proposals.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The budget is an important instrument of fiscal policy and provides information about government finances and spending priorities.

notes_list.title: Revenue and Capital Expenditure
notes_list.basic_overview: Government expenditure is broadly classified into revenue expenditure and capital expenditure according to the nature and accounting treatment of the expenditure.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Capital expenditure generally creates assets or reduces liabilities, while revenue expenditure generally relates to ongoing government operations and services.

notes_list.title: Public Debt
notes_list.basic_overview: Public debt represents the accumulated borrowing obligations of the government arising from past borrowing.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Government borrowing can finance public investment and fiscal deficits, while the sustainability of debt depends on factors including growth, interest costs and fiscal balances.
